headline: US Navy drone sailboat launches dual JAGM missiles in live-fire RIMPAC 2026 tests
summary: The Saildrone Surveyor SD-3001, co-developed with Lockheed Martin, successfully fired two Joint-Air-to-Ground Missiles during recent RIMPAC exercises near Hawaii. It also demonstrated electronic warfare capabilities.
details: The U.S. Navy successfully conducted live-fire tests with its Saildrone Surveyor SD-3001 Unmanned Surface Vessel (USV) during the RIMPAC 2026 exercises. Co-developed with Lockheed Martin, the drone sailboat launched two combat-proven Joint-Air-to-Ground Missiles (JAGM) near Hawaii.

The Saildrone was integrated with the USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) Carrier Strike Group, marking its first use as a combat asset. Under ARES control, the USV demonstrated its ability to deploy lethal JAGM missiles, which feature dual guidance modes for all-weather effectiveness.

Development of the Saildrone Surveyor SD-3001 with JAGM integration was rapid, achieving operational proof within six months of the collaborative project's start in October 2025. This swift progress included integrating the USV into the Navy fleet environment.

Beyond missile deployment, the autonomous Saildrone also proved its electronic warfare (EW) capabilities. It successfully coordinated sensors with an MH-60S helicopter to detect, classify, and identify a surrogate threat.

Lockheed Martin, Saildrone, and the U.S. Navy plan further tests and trials for this USV. This successful demonstration de-risks larger payload integrations for the upcoming Saildrone Spectre, which is expected to carry significantly larger containerized capabilities.

headline_marked: Generative AI [[eliminates obvious phishing clues]], enabling hyper-realistic multi-channel scams
headline: Generative AI eliminates obvious phishing clues, enabling hyper-realistic multi-channel scams
summary: Generative AI has made traditional phishing detection methods obsolete by eliminating grammatical errors and enabling sophisticated voice cloning and hyper-personalized attacks across multiple platforms.
details: Phishing emails were once easy to spot by typos and generic greetings, a focus of cybersecurity training. Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs) have completely changed this landscape, rewriting the rules of social engineering.

AI removes the bottleneck for threat actors, allowing them to automate hyper-personalization at scale. LLMs can generate dozens of contextually flawless lures in seconds, a task that previously took human analysts hours.
This shift introduces native-language fluency, automated OSINT for weaving real details into lures, and behavioral A/B testing to optimize scam effectiveness before mass deployment.
Phishing now extends beyond email to Slack, Microsoft Teams, SMS, and voice calls. Multimodal AI is weaponized across the entire corporate ecosystem, targeting various communication channels.

Voice cloning tools can replicate a person's cadence, accent, and emotional inflection from as little as 30 seconds of audio. This makes urgent demands, like wire transfers from a "boss," incredibly convincing, often overriding human trust-wiring.

Relying on employees to "stay vigilant" is no longer effective when scams are perfectly formatted, contextually accurate, and timed to real financial cycles. Expecting a human to catch the deception is a losing battle.

Effective defense requires shifting from human intuition to process-driven zero trust. Implementing strict verified callback rules for sensitive transactions can instantly nullify voice cloning and email spoofing.
Defenders are also using behavioral AI and machine learning to scan for anomalies in communication patterns, domain reputation, and contextual metadata in real time, catching what human eyes miss.
Modern security awareness programs must simulate the psychological pressure and realistic, multi-channel nature of today's AI threats, moving beyond outdated typo-spotting exercises.
